column1: Cleopatra lived closer to the Moon landing than to the pyramids
column2: The Great Pyramid of Giza was finished around 2560 BC. Cleopatra died in 30 BC, roughly 2,500 years later, and the Moon landing came about 2,000 years after her.
column3: Ancient Egypt was already ancient to the ancient Egyptians.

column1: Oxford University is older than the Aztec Empire
column2: Teaching at Oxford was underway by 1096. The Aztec city of Tenochtitlan was founded in 1325, more than two centuries later.
column3: Old and "new" world timelines overlap in surprising ways.

column1: The shortest war lasted under an hour
column2: The Anglo-Zanzibar War of 27 August 1896 ended after roughly 38 to 45 minutes of British naval bombardment. The Sultan's palace was wrecked and a pro-British ruler installed.
column3: Power gaps can make conflicts brutally brief.

column1: Napoleon was not unusually short
column2: He was about 5 feet 7 inches, average for a Frenchman of his time. The myth grew from confusion between French and English inches and from British cartoons mocking him.
column3: Propaganda can outlive the person it targets.

column1: The Great Fire of London had few recorded deaths
column2: The 1666 fire destroyed around 13,000 houses and St Paul's Cathedral, yet only a handful of deaths were officially recorded. Historians think the true toll among the poor was higher but went uncounted.
column3: Who gets counted shapes what history remembers.

column1: Vikings did not wear horned helmets
column2: No horned helmet has been found from a Viking-age warrior grave. The image comes largely from 19th-century art and costume design, including Wagner's opera productions.
column3: Much of our picture of the past is Victorian stagecraft.

column1: The printing press spread faster than you would think
column2: Gutenberg printed his Bible around 1455. By 1500, presses operated in more than 250 European towns and had produced millions of books.
column3: New information technology has always spread fast.

column1: Ancient Romans used a kind of concrete that lasts
column2: Roman builders mixed lime with volcanic ash. Some harbour structures have survived 2,000 years of seawater, and researchers think minerals growing inside the concrete help seal cracks.
column3: Old techniques can still teach modern engineers.

column1: The Hundred Years' War lasted 116 years
column2: The conflict between England and France ran from 1337 to 1453. It was a series of wars broken by truces, not one continuous fight.
column3: Historians name periods after the fact, not neatly.

column1: Tsar Peter the Great taxed beards
column2: In 1698 Peter imposed a tax on beards to push Russian nobles towards Western European fashion. Payers carried a token proving they had paid.
column3: Rulers have long used taxes to change behaviour.

column1: The Black Death killed around a third of Europe
column2: Between 1347 and 1351 plague swept Europe, killing an estimated 30 to 50 percent of the population. Labour shortages afterwards pushed up wages for surviving workers.
column3: Catastrophes can shift economic power.

column1: The Eiffel Tower was meant to be temporary
column2: Built for the 1889 World's Fair, it had a 20-year permit. It was saved partly because it proved useful as a radio transmission tower.
column3: Usefulness is a strong defence against demolition.

column1: Ancient Olympians competed naked
column2: In the ancient Greek Games, male athletes competed nude. The word "gymnasium" comes from the Greek "gymnos", meaning naked.
column3: Words carry fossils of old customs.

column1: The Rosetta Stone unlocked hieroglyphs
column2: Found in 1799, the stone carries the same decree in hieroglyphs, Demotic and Ancient Greek. Jean-François Champollion used it to announce his decipherment in 1822.
column3: One translated text can open a whole lost language.

column1: Mammoths were still alive when the pyramids were built
column2: A small population of woolly mammoths survived on Wrangel Island in the Arctic until about 4,000 years ago. The Great Pyramid was built around 4,500 years ago.
column3: Extinction is often a slow fade, not a single event.

column1: The first known strike was in ancient Egypt
column2: Around 1157 BC, tomb builders at Deir el-Medina stopped work because their grain rations were late. Records of the protest survive on papyrus.
column3: Workers have bargained over pay for over 3,000 years.

column1: The Library of Alexandria declined slowly
column2: There was no single fire that destroyed everything. The library faded over centuries through funding cuts, political purges and several conflicts.
column3: Institutions usually die from neglect, not drama.

column1: Sliced bread was briefly banned in the US
column2: In January 1943 the US banned sliced bread to save resources during the war. Public outcry got the ban lifted within about two months.
column3: Small comforts can carry big political weight.

column1: Medieval people did not think the Earth was flat
column2: Educated Europeans in the Middle Ages generally knew the Earth was round. The flat-Earth myth about them was popularised in the 1800s.
column3: Each era likes to think the last was more ignorant.

column1: The Great Wall is not visible from the Moon
column2: It is very long but only a few metres wide. Astronauts have confirmed it cannot be seen with the naked eye from the Moon.
column3: Big claims deserve a quick check.

column1: Coffee houses were nicknamed penny universities
column2: In 17th-century England, a penny bought entry and coffee, plus hours of debate and news. Lloyd's of London began in Edward Lloyd's coffee house.
column3: Shared spaces can incubate whole industries.

column1: Paper money started in China
column2: China was using paper money by the Song dynasty in the 11th century. Europe did not adopt banknotes widely until the 1600s.
column3: Many "modern" inventions are centuries old.

column1: The Titanic's sister ship had a long career
column2: RMS Olympic, Titanic's near-identical sister, served from 1911 to 1935. She was nicknamed "Old Reliable" and even rammed a German U-boat in 1918.
column3: Fame often goes to the disaster, not the success.

column1: The Aztec capital was built on a lake
column2: Tenochtitlan stood on islands in Lake Texcoco, linked by causeways. Mexico City sits on the drained lakebed and is sinking as a result.
column3: Cities inherit the choices of their founders.

column1: The Romans had fast food counters
column2: Pompeii had dozens of thermopolia, street counters serving hot food and drink. Many Romans in cramped flats had no kitchen of their own.
column3: Eating out is as old as city living.

column1: The ancient Greeks had a vending machine
column2: Hero of Alexandria described a coin-operated device in the first century AD. A coin dropped onto a lever released a measured amount of holy water.
column3: Clever automation is older than electricity.

column1: Cats were sacred in ancient Egypt
column2: Egyptians linked cats with the goddess Bastet. Killing one, even by accident, could bring severe punishment, and many cats were mummified.
column3: What a culture protects reveals what it values.

column1: The first speeding ticket was for 8 mph
column2: In 1896 Walter Arnold was fined in Kent for driving at about 8 mph, four times the limit of 2 mph in town. A man with a flag was supposed to walk ahead of cars.
column3: Every new technology outpaces its rules.

column1: Queen Victoria's reign was not the longest British reign
column2: Victoria reigned for 63 years. Elizabeth II overtook her in 2015 and reigned for 70 years.
column3: Records are made to be broken, eventually.

column1: The Spanish flu probably did not start in Spain
column2: Spain was neutral in the First World War and reported the 1918 flu openly. Countries at war censored news, so it looked like Spain was hit first.
column3: Who reports a story can shape its name.

column1: Ancient Romans used urine to clean clothes
column2: Urine contains ammonia, which helps lift grease and dirt. Laundries called fullonicae collected it from public pots, and it was even taxed.
column3: Yesterday's waste was someone's raw material.

column1: The Statue of Liberty was a gift from France
column2: It was designed by Frédéric Auguste Bartholdi and dedicated in 1886. Gustave Eiffel's company engineered its internal iron framework.
column3: Friendship between nations can be cast in copper.

column1: The Statue of Liberty used to be brown
column2: It is covered in copper, which was originally a shiny reddish-brown. Over about 20 years, weathering turned it green.
column3: Time changes even monuments.

column1: Ancient Egyptians used stone pillows
column2: Wealthier Egyptians slept with their heads on curved headrests made of wood or stone. They raised the head and may have kept insects away.
column3: Comfort is shaped by climate and culture.

column1: The first Olympic marathon winner was a water carrier
column2: Spyridon Louis won the marathon at the 1896 Athens Olympics. He became a national hero in Greece.
column3: Ordinary people can make extraordinary history.

column1: London's Big Ben is a bell, not the tower
column2: Big Ben is the nickname of the great bell. The tower was renamed the Elizabeth Tower in 2012.
column3: Nicknames often stick to the wrong thing.

column1: Medieval castles were often colourful
column2: Many castle walls were whitewashed or painted, and interiors were bright with colour. We picture them grey because the paint has worn away.
column3: Ruins hide how vivid the past was.

column1: The Mayflower later became a barn, some say
column2: A popular story claims the Mayflower's timbers were reused in a barn in Buckinghamshire. Historians consider the link possible but unproven.
column3: Not every good story can be verified.

column1: Abacus users can still beat calculators
column2: Skilled abacus users can do arithmetic extremely fast. In a 1946 contest in Tokyo, an abacus user beat an electric calculator in most rounds.
column3: Practised skill can rival machines.

column1: The Romans did not use the number zero
column2: Roman numerals have no symbol for zero. The concept of zero as a number came from India and spread through the Arab world.
column3: Some ideas are invented, not discovered.

column1: Pirates rarely buried treasure
column2: Most pirates spent or traded their loot quickly. The buried treasure idea was popularised by the novel Treasure Island in 1883.
column3: Fiction can shape how we imagine history.

column1: Ancient Greek statues were painted
column2: Traces of pigment show many Greek statues were brightly coloured. The pure white marble look we admire came later as paint wore off.
column3: The past was more colourful than we think.

column1: The Leaning Tower of Pisa leaned during construction
column2: Building began in 1173, and the tower started tilting before it was finished because of soft ground. Builders tried to compensate by making upper floors slightly taller on one side.
column3: Mistakes can become icons.

column1: Before alarm clocks there were knocker-ups
column2: In industrial Britain, people were paid to wake workers by tapping on windows with long poles or shooting peas at them.
column3: Every problem creates a job.

column1: Lincoln was a licensed bartender
column2: Abraham Lincoln co-owned a store in New Salem, Illinois, which got a licence to sell liquor in 1833.
column3: Leaders often have surprising early careers.

column1: The first known map of the world is Babylonian
column2: The Babylonian Map of the World, a clay tablet from around the 6th century BC, shows Babylon at the centre surrounded by water.
column3: Maps show beliefs as much as places.

column1: The Ottoman Empire lasted over 600 years
column2: Founded around 1299, it ended in 1922. At its peak it stretched across parts of Europe, Asia and Africa.
column3: Empires can last longer than nations exist today.

column1: Silk was a closely guarded Chinese secret
column2: For centuries China kept silk-making secret. Byzantine monks are said to have smuggled silkworm eggs to the West around 550 AD.
column3: Industrial secrets have always been worth stealing.

column1: The Hanseatic League was a medieval trade network
column2: From the 13th to 17th centuries, towns across northern Europe joined forces to protect trade. It controlled much of Baltic commerce.
column3: Cooperation can be as powerful as empire.

column1: Tea was once used as money
column2: In parts of Asia, compressed tea bricks were used as currency. They could be traded, or eaten and drunk if needed.
column3: Money is whatever people agree to accept.

column1: The Gregorian calendar skipped days
column2: When Catholic countries adopted it in 1582, 10 days were skipped. Britain switched in 1752 and skipped 11 days.
column3: Even time can be rearranged by decree.

column1: Ancient Rome had a population of about a million
column2: At its height around the 2nd century AD, Rome may have had up to a million people. No European city matched that again until London in the 1800s.
column3: Cities can shrink as well as grow.

column1: The Battle of Hastings was not at Hastings
column2: It was fought in 1066 about 10 kilometres away, at what is now the town of Battle. The abbey there marks the spot.
column3: Names drift from the places they describe.

column1: The Magna Carta was mostly repealed
column2: Of its original clauses, only three remain part of English law. Its lasting power is as a symbol of limits on power.
column3: Symbols can outlast the text behind them.

column1: Thomas Edison did not invent the light bulb
column2: Many inventors made electric lights before him. Edison's team made a practical, long-lasting bulb and a system to power it.
column3: Winning often means improving, not inventing.

column1: The first photograph took hours to expose
column2: Nicéphore Niépce's view from a window, made around 1826–27, needed an exposure of many hours, possibly days.
column3: Instant was once unimaginable.

column1: Ancient Persians had refrigerators
column2: Yakhchals were domed structures that stored ice through hot desert summers using shade, insulation and evaporation.
column3: Clever design can beat harsh climates.

column1: Women in Britain first voted nationally in 1918
column2: The Representation of the People Act 1918 gave some women over 30 the vote. Equal voting with men came in 1928.
column3: Rights often arrive in stages.

column1: Tutankhamun's tomb was found nearly intact
column2: Howard Carter found it in 1922. Most Egyptian royal tombs had been robbed long before.
column3: Being forgotten can protect you.

column1: The first email was sent in 1971
column2: Ray Tomlinson sent it between two computers next to each other. He chose the @ sign to separate user and machine names.
column3: Big shifts can start with small tests.

column1: The Inca kept records with knots
column2: Quipu were cords with knots that recorded numbers and possibly other information. Experts still debate how much they could record.
column3: Writing is not the only way to remember.

column1: Gladiators were not always fought to the death
column2: Gladiators were expensive to train, and many bouts ended without a death. A defeated fighter could be spared.
column3: Spectacle and economics are often linked.

column1: The Berlin Wall fell partly by mistake
column2: On 9 November 1989, an East German spokesman wrongly said new travel rules applied immediately. Crowds gathered at the border, and guards opened the gates.
column3: History can turn on one confused announcement.

column1: Ancient Mesopotamians invented the 60-minute hour
column2: The Babylonians used a base-60 number system. That is why we have 60 seconds in a minute and 360 degrees in a circle.
column3: Old maths still runs our clocks.

column1: Lady Godiva's ride may be a legend
column2: The story of her riding naked through Coventry first appears long after her death. Historians doubt it happened.
column3: Legends can attach to real people.

column1: The Great Stink pushed London to build sewers
column2: In the hot summer of 1858, the stench from the Thames was so bad that Parliament acted. Joseph Bazalgette's sewers followed.
column3: Crisis can force overdue change.

column1: The ancient Greeks invented the Olympics in 776 BC
column2: The first recorded Games at Olympia had one event, a short foot race. More events were added over centuries.
column3: Big traditions can start small.

column1: Chess was once played with different rules
column2: The queen used to be a weak piece. Around 1475, rules in Spain made her the most powerful piece, speeding up the game.
column3: Games evolve to stay exciting.

column1: The first vaccine came from cowpox
column2: In 1796 Edward Jenner showed that cowpox could protect against smallpox. The word vaccine comes from the Latin "vacca", meaning cow.
column3: Breakthroughs can come from careful observation.

column1: Smallpox is the only human disease eradicated
column2: The WHO declared smallpox eradicated in 1980 after a global vaccination campaign. It had killed hundreds of millions.
column3: Global cooperation can end a plague.

column1: The first postage stamp was the Penny Black
column2: Issued in Britain in 1840, it let the sender prepay postage. Before, the receiver often paid.
column3: Small fixes can transform a system.

column1: Ancient Egyptians invented toothpaste of a kind
column2: They used mixtures that included powdered ox hooves, ashes and eggshells. It was rough but helped clean teeth.
column3: Hygiene is an ancient pursuit.

column1: The longest-reigning monarch ruled 72 years
column2: Louis XIV of France reigned from 1643 to 1715, starting at age four. He built the Palace of Versailles.
column3: Inheriting power young can mean holding it long.

column1: Medieval monks invented a form of champagne, by legend
column2: Dom Pérignon is often credited, but sparkling wine existed before him. He worked to improve wine quality.
column3: Credit often goes to the famous name.

column1: Venice was built on wooden piles
column2: Millions of wooden stakes driven into the mud support the city. Underwater and without oxygen, the wood has lasted for centuries.
column3: Hidden foundations hold up whole cities.

column1: The Wright brothers' first flight lasted 12 seconds
column2: On 17 December 1903, Orville Wright flew about 37 metres. Later that day Wilbur flew 260 metres in 59 seconds.
column3: The beginning of something huge can look tiny.

column1: Ancient Rome had a central heating system
column2: Wealthy Romans used the hypocaust, which circulated hot air under floors and inside walls.
column3: Comfort engineering has a long history.

column1: The Taj Mahal took about 20 years to build
column2: Mughal emperor Shah Jahan ordered it in memory of his wife Mumtaz Mahal. Around 20,000 workers were involved.
column3: Grief can inspire great works.

column1: The Domesday Book was a royal survey
column2: In 1086 William the Conqueror ordered a survey of land and property across much of England. It recorded about 13,000 places.
column3: Governments have always wanted data.

column1: The first British banknotes were handwritten
column2: The Bank of England, founded in 1694, issued handwritten notes for specific amounts. Fully printed notes came later.
column3: Trust in paper had to be built.

column1: Hadrian's Wall stretched coast to coast
column2: Built from AD 122, it ran about 117 kilometres across northern England. It had forts, gates and watchtowers along its length.
column3: Borders have long been built in stone.

column1: The Great Pyramid was the tallest structure for millennia
column2: At about 146 metres originally, it was the tallest human-made structure for around 3,800 years. Lincoln Cathedral's spire overtook it around 1311.
column3: Some records last almost forever.

column1: Ancient Rome had a fire brigade
column2: Emperor Augustus created the Vigiles in AD 6. They fought fires and patrolled the streets at night.
column3: Public services grow with cities.

column1: The first public museum opened in Oxford
column2: The Ashmolean Museum opened in 1683. It is often called Britain's first public museum.
column3: Knowledge became public property slowly.

column1: Spartan boys started military training at seven
column2: In ancient Sparta, boys entered the agoge, a tough state training programme. It shaped them into soldiers.
column3: Societies raise people for their priorities.

column1: Ancient Chinese used dragon bones to find writing
column2: In 1899, scholars noticed inscriptions on "dragon bones" sold as medicine. They were oracle bones, the earliest known Chinese writing.
column3: Treasure can hide in plain sight.
